newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish doctors launch strike over pay, funding.
newsitem.headline: Polish doctors launch strike over pay, funding.

text.p: A union grouping one third of Poland's 90,000 doctors launched a strike on Tuesday for more pay and funding for the creaking health service, despite controversy over the ethics of their action.
The All-Poland Doctors' Union (OZZL) began the protest after the latest meeting in two months of negotiations with the government ended in deadlock on Monday.

The doctors are continuing to treat emergency and life threatening cases and have excluded cancer, psychiatric, children's and maternity wards from the stoppage, but routine examinations and operations are being cancelled.

Union chiefs said it was too early to measure the extent of the protest, but treasurer Dariusz Rapajczak told Reuters that doctors at about three quarters of Poland's hospitals and half of outpatient clinics had voted to back it.
The doctors want budget spending on the health service to rise to six percent of gross domestic product next year, while the government plans to allocate 4.5 percent.
They seek a collective wage deal, for doctors only, which would increase their monthly salaries to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) -- three times the average industrial wage.
They also back the Solidarity trade union federation's proposals for a reform of the health insurance system.

Solidarity, Poland's biggest union, said it backed most of the strike's aims and its members were free to join the protest, although the union wants a collective pay deal for all health workers including nurses and technicians, not just doctors.
Solidarity's leadership was meeting in the port city of Gdansk to decide further tactics.
Some prominent doctors questioned the strike's ethics, while strongly supporting its aims.

Opposition politician Zofia Kuratowska, a working doctor and deputy speaker of Poland's Senate, told the pro-government daily Trybuna that doctors were right to hold demonstrations or refuse to fill out bureaucratic forms in protest.
But she said: "In my view this strike is absolutely in contradiction with medical ethics."
The OZZL union's Rapajczak rejected such arguments, accusing the government of underfunding health and failing to ensure proper free treatment, guaranteed by the constitution.

"The main point (of the strike) is to harm patients as little as possible. But it is common for patients to wait half a year for some procedures and no-one is saying that this is immoral," Rapajczak said.
